mech: Newcomen engines burned so much fuel that they paid only where coal was almost free, as at British pitheads; cheap coal made the engine worth building and then improving.
After Watt's separate condenser cut fuel use, steam freed mills, mines and ironworks from rivers and later drove railways.
Allen calculates that the spinning jenny paid a high return where labour was dear relative to capital, as in England, and little or nothing in France or India.
The jenny was worked by women and children whose pay was low; using a male building labourer's day wage overstates the labour cost the machine saved.
Dear labour beside cheap coal rewarded machines that swapped fuel for muscle.
Crafts' revised national accounts show income per head growing slowly before 1830: a few sectors, cotton above all, were transformed while most of the economy changed little.
An industrial enlightenment of societies, journals, lectures and encyclopedias cut the cost of finding out what was known, so improvements could build on one another.
Watt refined the engine as instrument maker to Glasgow University, among Joseph Black's chemists and later the Lunar Society: Mokyr's case of knowledge moving between savants and makers.
Cheap print, technical dictionaries and public lectures spread technique among craftsmen.
Mechanisation spread fastest where pools of skilled mechanics already existed, people who could build the new machines and keep them running.
Clockmakers and millwrights turned inventions like the water frame into working factory machinery.
British wages were high because workers were better fed, taller and more skilled: a sign of productivity rather than a cost that pushed firms to mechanise.
Coal broke the limit of the organic economy, where all heat and power came from what plants captured from the sun on a fixed area of land.
Britain's coal lay near London and navigable water; China's lay in the north-west, far from the Yangzi delta, its most commercial region.
New World land and slave labour supplied cotton, sugar and timber that would otherwise have needed millions of English acres.
Atlantic markets built on enslaved African labour bought the export manufactures in which British mechanisation first took hold.
The labour of enslaved Africans produced the sugar, tobacco and cotton at the heart of Atlantic commerce.

Williams argued that profits of the slave trade and plantations financed British industry; critics say those profits were too small a share of investment, and Inikori recasts the case as one about demand.
Protection from Indian calicoes, and the challenge of matching Indian quality, pushed British makers to mechanise spinning.
The rich left more surviving children, whose downward mobility spread literacy, thrift and patience through the population until efficiency could grow.
Sustained productivity growth spread from Britain to western Europe and North America; by 1913 British income per head was about eight times China's in the Maddison Project figures.
Before 1800 average incomes everywhere stayed near subsistence because population growth ate every gain; sustained efficiency growth from the Industrial Revolution broke that link.
High-pressure steam engines on rails turned coal into cheap overland transport.

view: Broadberry, Campbell, Klein, Overton and van Leeuwen
mech: The plague roughly halved England's population; land per worker rose and so did output per head, and in England and Holland the gain was never lost.
Higher wages after the plague raised demand for town goods; cities and wars, both deadly, kept death rates high and so held incomes up: the 'three horsemen of riches'.
High post-plague wages, later marriage and strong demand for skills fed human capital, visible in soaring book production in the North Sea region.
Allen's series show London and Amsterdam labourers earning well above a respectable subsistence by 1700, while real wages in Florence, Vienna and Delhi sank back toward the bare-bones level.
Humphries and Weisdorf's annual-earnings series rise from the later seventeenth century as men worked more days a year, a pattern that fits an industrious revolution better than rising day wages.
Households that worked more for the market to buy tea, sugar, cloth and crockery created the demand that factories later supplied.
Atlantic trade enriched merchants most where monarchs were already checked, as in England and the Netherlands, and those merchants then pushed for better institutions.
Silver wages in the Yangzi delta and India were already well below England's by the seventeenth century, so the Great Divergence had early roots.
The core regions of China were comparable with England as late as about 1750, so earlier North Sea gains explain little of the later gap.
Necker financed the American war with loans rather than taxes, so interest charges swelled the deficit that Calonne finally admitted in 1786.
Calonne summoned notables to approve a land tax on all, hoping to bypass the parlements.
Notables and parlements insisted only the Estates-General could consent to new taxes; in August 1788 Brienne conceded and called it for May 1789.
With no body able to commit the nation to taxes, the crown could neither raise them nor keep borrowing; summoning the Estates was a bid for credible consent.
Bankruptcy, not a rising class, opened the door: once the monarchy had to ask for consent it lost control of the agenda.
A dry, hot spring and early summer stunted the grain before the harvest.
The storms of 13 July 1788 flattened ripe crops along a band of northern France days before reaping.
Grain prices climbed through autumn and winter; Rudé estimated that at the peak bread could swallow most of a Paris labourer's earnings.
Frozen rivers and mills cut flour deliveries to Paris and stopped outdoor work, so prices rose as earnings fell.
Cheaper British cloth hit French textile towns in 1787-89, adding unemployment to dear bread.
The April 1789 riot followed the report that the manufacturer Réveillon had said a worker could live on 15 sous a day, when the loaf cost 14.5.
The crowd of 14 July was largely Paris craftsmen and journeymen, and the loaf stood at its peak that day.
Deadlock over voting by order led the Third Estate to declare itself the National Assembly and swear not to disperse.
The Assembly's defiance, the king's troop build-up and Necker's dismissal on 11 July made Parisians arm, and they went to the Bastille for powder.
News from Paris and fear of an aristocratic plot travelled along with rumours of hired brigands.
Hunger and vagrancy in the weeks before the new harvest made every band of strangers look like brigands come to cut the green corn.
With chateaux burning, deputies abolished feudal privileges to calm the countryside.
Market women who marched on 5 October demanded bread and brought the royal family back to Paris.
A bourgeoisie enriched by the century's commercial boom, colonial trade above all, resented the privileges of the nobility and seized power.
Commercial growth built a confident professional and consumer middle class and a public sphere that came to demand representation.
The language of popular sovereignty and the general will, not class interest, drove the Revolution from consent to Terror.
Revolutionary deputies were lawyers and office-holders steeped in reforming ideas, not capitalist manufacturers: the class story does not fit who made 1789.
The Assembly nationalised church land in November 1789 and issued assignats against it; war deficits turned them into unbacked paper.
Revolutionary leaders sought war in 1792 to unmask traitors and export liberty; monarchs feared contagion.
War spending from 1792 was paid for by printing assignats until they were nearly worthless in 1796.

The largest eruption in recorded history put a sulphate veil in the stratosphere; in 1816 western and central Europe and north-eastern America had cold, wet summers with frosts, on top of a decade already cooled by an eruption of 1809.
Stratospheric aerosol cooling brought killing frosts to New England in June, July and August 1816.
Cold and rain delayed and rotted grain, potatoes and grapes; Swiss, south German and French harvests failed worst.
Grain prices roughly doubled in much of western Europe by spring 1817, bringing begging, disease and excess deaths.
Demobilised soldiers, war debts and the postwar slump left workers jobless and governments poor just as the harvest failed.
Starving families from Württemberg, Baden and Switzerland floated down the Rhine to Dutch ports, bound for America.
Cold summers ruined three rice harvests in Yunnan, where families sold children and farmers turned to opium.
A disrupted monsoon in Bengal in 1816-17 may have favoured the new cholera strain that broke out of the Ganges delta in 1817.
Rain kept Byron's party indoors at Geneva in June 1816; a ghost-story contest there produced the tale that became Frankenstein.
An acre or two of potatoes could feed a family, so couples married young and population grew from about 2.5 to over 8 million.
A population pressing on subsistence was due a positive check; Mokyr found no link between county population density and famine deaths, which undercuts the claim.
Poverty, not numbers, made Ireland vulnerable: the poorest third lived almost entirely on potatoes, with no savings or other food to fall back on.
Blight destroyed about a third of the 1845 crop and three-quarters of 1846; little was planted in 1847 and the crop failed again in 1848.
The same blight hit the Scottish Highlands, but relief and landlord support kept deaths far lower than in Ireland.
Crowding on public works, in soup queues and workhouses spread lice-borne typhus and relapsing fever among the weakened.
Roughly a million people left in the famine years, many on overcrowded ships to Liverpool, Canada and the United States.
Task wages on the works fell behind soaring food prices, and hard outdoor labour in the bitter winter of 1846-47 wore down the starving.
Free rations for about three million people a day were the most effective relief of the famine; they were wound down in September 1847.
Tenants had to give up land to get relief, and landlords facing poor-rate bills cleared their estates.
Putting relief on local poor rates starved the bankrupt western unions of funds just as need peaked in 1848-49.
Evicted families and assisted emigrants filled the ships from western estates.
Oats, wheat and cattle kept leaving Irish ports while people starved, and the government refused to close them.
The grain exported in 1846-47 was small beside the lost potato crop and was outweighed by maize imports; an export ban would have helped at the margin only.
Peel used the Irish crisis to carry repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, at the cost of his party.
The 1876-77 El Niño brought monsoon failure to the Deccan and Madras.
The same ocean warming brought drought to Shanxi, Henan, Shandong and Zhili.
Drought struck Ceará and the north-eastern sertão, sending refugees to Fortaleza.
Sir Richard Temple's ration of one pound of grain a day for heavy labour on relief works, and distance tests for relief, turned scarcity into mass death.
Officials designed relief to avoid 'demoralising' dependency, so it was set to deter the hungry rather than save them.
Grain left famine districts for ports and abroad while the government refused to interfere with trade.
Railways let merchants move grain out of drought districts to towns and ports where it fetched more.
In districts linked by rail, rainfall shortfalls raised local prices and mortality much less, because grain could come in.
Ever-normal granaries that had carried eighteenth-century provinces through droughts were empty or gone by the 1870s.
Wars against the Taiping and Nian drained the treasury and pulled revenue and attention from the north China relief system.
The scandal of 1876-78 produced the Famine Commission of 1880 and codes that told officials when and how to relieve.
War spending and procurement drove food prices beyond what rural labourers could pay, though food available in Bengal was not far below normal years.
A famine that killed around three million people destroyed what remained of Britain's claim to govern Bengal well.
Germany's battle fleet convinced Britain that Berlin was its chief threat and drew it toward France and Russia.
Two armed blocs meant a Balkan quarrel could become a continental war within days.
Facing two fronts, German planners chose to knock France out first by marching through Belgium.
Annexation humiliated Russia and Serbia and fed the Serbian nationalist networks, including the Black Hand, that armed the Sarajevo assassins.
Serbia nearly doubled its territory, convincing Vienna that South Slav nationalism threatened the monarchy's existence.
Vienna sent Count Hoyos to Berlin on 5 July 1914 and came back with a promise of full support.
Berlin promised support and urged speed, accepting that Russia might intervene.
Vienna resolved on war with Serbia for its own reasons; Berlin's backing enabled the decision rather than caused it.
Russia began its 'period preparatory to war' on 25-26 July, before Austria had mobilised against it, with an eye on the Straits.
Russian leaders, reassured by Poincaré's visit to St Petersburg on 20-23 July, chose early military measures to back Serbia.
Germany's only plan required an immediate attack in the west once Russia mobilised, so railway timetables turned mobilisation into war.
German leaders used the crisis to start a war they judged winnable before Russia's rearmament was complete.
The violation of Belgian neutrality brought Britain into the war on 4 August.
Millions of casualties, inflation and Petrograd bread queues broke the tsarist regime in February 1917 and the Provisional Government by October.
The Bolshevik seizure of power and victory in the civil war produced the Soviet state.
Victory let the Allies dictate terms to Germany at Paris.
Keynes argued that reparations beyond Germany's capacity to pay would wreck European recovery.
The war broke the pre-1914 gold standard; the restored system had misaligned parities, scarce gold and less credible commitments.
Under gold, deflation spread from country to country and no central bank could expand without losing reserves.
Temin's later view: the gold-standard mentality made deflation the policy everywhere until countries abandoned it.
American loans recycled reparations; when lending stopped in 1928 Germany was squeezed and no country would act as lender of last resort.
Higher rates meant to cool speculation slowed the economy before the crash.
Rising US rates pulled gold from Europe and forced foreign central banks to tighten too.
Uncertainty after the crash made households stop buying cars and other durables.
Consumer spending fell in 1930 by more than lost wealth or income can explain, and this real shock, not money, started the slide.
Panics made people hold cash and banks hold reserves, so the money stock fell by about a third while the Fed did not offset it.
Bank failures destroyed lenders' knowledge of their borrowers, so credit to farmers, households and small firms dried up beyond any effect through money.
The tariff cut imports and invited retaliation but explains only a small part of the fall in output.
Runs spread from Vienna as foreign creditors pulled funds from central Europe.
London's claims frozen in Germany set off the run on sterling.
Countries recovered in the order they left gold: Britain and Scandinavia from 1931-32, the gold bloc not until 1935-36.
Erosion permanently lowered farm values in the worst-hit Plains counties, and adjustment came mostly through people leaving.
Nazi votes rose most among groups hurt by the slump but not jobless themselves, such as the self-employed and shopkeepers; the unemployed leaned Communist.
Towns more exposed to the failed Danatbank saw larger Nazi vote gains.
Within two months the cabinet won power to rule by decree.
Rearmament and expansion for living space in the east were core aims of Hitler's regime.
An 'eliminationist' antisemitism shared by most Germans made ordinary men willing killers.
Perpetrators killed with zeal because they believed Jews deserved to die.
At Józefów only about a dozen of some 500 men of Police Battalion 101 stepped out when offered; conformity, deference and careerism explain more than hatred.
Racial antisemitism, the regime's creed, was written into law as citizenship and marriage bans.
Destruction followed a bureaucratic sequence: definition, expropriation, concentration, annihilation; the legal definition of a Jew was the first step.
Persecution radicalised in steps, from legal exclusion to open violence and forced emigration.
After the pogrom the state took over Jewish property and pushed emigration, showing that open violence met little resistance at home.
Hitler's long-held aim of destroying the Jews, announced in his Reichstag 'prophecy' of January 1939, was carried out when war gave cover.
Hitler's ideological goals set the direction; officials 'working towards the Führer' competed to radicalise policy without waiting for orders.
Conquering Poland put about two million Jews under German rule; the fall of France made Madagascar look available.
Each failed deportation scheme left Jews crammed in ghettos, and rival agencies radicalised to solve a problem they had made themselves.
From late July and August 1941 the shootings widened from Jewish men to women and children.
Mass shooting killed well over a million Jews in the occupied Soviet territories, and its scale showed the killers what was possible.
Planners meant to divert Soviet food to Germany; besieged Leningrad and some three million Soviet prisoners of war were starved.
When the Hunger Plan could not be carried out in full, Jews were redefined as the surplus mouths to be removed first.
Most victims lived where Soviet and then German occupation destroyed every state that might have protected them.
Browning dates the decision to murder all of Europe's Jews to the euphoria of victory in October 1941, after the shootings had shown the way.
Once Germany declared war on the United States, Hitler told party leaders on 12 December 1941 that the Jews would be annihilated; Wannsee organised it.
Belzec began gassing in March 1942, Sobibor and Treblinka followed.
Where the Red Army stood in 1945, communist regimes followed.
Yalta's promises of free elections in Poland went unkept, and Western leaders read that as bad faith.
Soviet conduct in Poland, Iran and Turkey readied Washington for a hard reading of Moscow.
Kennan's diagnosis gave officials the logic of containment: Soviet power yields to firm counter-pressure.
Soviet pressure on Greece and Turkey after the takeover of eastern Europe forced an American response.
The United States needed open markets in Europe; aid tied to open trade was something Stalin could not accept, and Molotov walked out of the Paris talks in July 1947.
Western currency reform in June 1948 and plans for a West German state set off the blockade.
Fearing Soviet gains from postwar chaos more than Soviet attack, Washington sought a preponderance of power, which Moscow read as encirclement.
The bomb was used partly to impress Moscow, and atomic diplomacy deepened Soviet distrust.
The airlift and the founding of NATO in 1949 fixed the division of Germany and Europe.
Two universal ideologies of modernity, each sure history was on its side, competed to remake the world.
With the Soviet archives open, Gaddis concluded that a cold war was unavoidable while Stalin ruled.
Stalin's revolutionary-imperial outlook sought security by control of neighbours, which the West could only read as expansion.
With Mao victorious, Stalin approved Kim Il-sung's invasion of the South in spring 1950.
The war militarised containment and spread it to Asia.
New states became the main arena where Washington and Moscow intervened to prove their models of development.
Moscow intervened to save a failing communist regime and keep Afghanistan from turning to the West.
The war cost lives, money and the Red Army's prestige and fed public cynicism under glasnost.
Hard currency from oil paid for grain imports; when the price fell, Moscow borrowed until lenders stopped.
An empire dependent on oil revenue and imported grain lost the means to buy loyalty.
Lower oil prices hurt, but the deficit grew mainly from choices such as the anti-alcohol campaign, which cut tax revenue, and rising subsidies.
Enterprises given freedom raised wages, while farm, industrial and military lobbies blocked the price reform that might have balanced them.
Open speech lifted fear, and each successful protest made the next one more likely: a tide of nationalism.
Gorbachev's choice to open politics, not economic decline, made the system's breakdown possible.
Gorbachev would not use force to save eastern European regimes, so they fell within months.
Eastern Europe's peaceful exits emboldened the Baltic and other republican movements.
Empty shops and lost central control convinced hardliners that only emergency rule could save the Union.
The plotters struck on the eve of the signing of a new Union Treaty that would have handed power to the republics.
Ukraine declared independence on 24 August, three days after the coup failed, and put it to a vote.
Without Ukraine, Yeltsin would not keep a Union in which Russia faced the Central Asian republics alone.
Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and the red flag came down over the Kremlin.
Reforms dismantled the party's command over the economy, and officials and republic elites took the assets and walked away.
Shortages and inflation destroyed faith in the centre and gave republics reason to keep their own resources.
Provincial autonomy and the 1937 Congress ministries persuaded the League that majority rule at the centre would leave Muslims a permanent minority.
Jinnah's deliberately vague 'Pakistan' rallied Muslims behind the League as their sole spokesman.
In the United Provinces, ulama and League workers sold Pakistan as a sovereign Islamic state, a "new Medina", and voters understood it as such.
The Viceroy declared India at war without consultation in 1939; Congress ministries resigned, and the Japanese advance of 1942 sharpened the demand.
With Congress leaders jailed from 1942 to 1945, the League built its organisation unopposed.
The war turned India from Britain's debtor into its creditor and left Britain without the will or troops to hold it.
Exhausted European powers faced nationalist movements the war had strengthened and two superpowers hostile to old empires.
Japan's conquests of 1942 shattered British, Dutch and French prestige in Asia beyond repair.
The League's near-sweep of Muslim seats forced London to offer a federation with Muslim-majority groups of provinces.
After Nehru said in July 1946 that Congress would not be bound by the plan's grouping scheme, the League withdrew its acceptance and called for Direct Action.
Congress preferred a strong centre over a weak union with parity, so it came to accept partition; Jinnah got the moth-eaten Pakistan he had not wanted.
Killing in Calcutta set off reprisals in Noakhali and Bihar and then in Punjab.
Spreading violence convinced British and Congress leaders that a united India could not be held together.
Bengal Hindu leaders demanded their own province rather than live under a Muslim-majority Bengal, and the plan partitioned the province.
The plan of 3 June set partition in motion and brought the handover forward to 15 August.
Ten weeks left no time to plan; no one knew where the border would run, and too few troops stood between armed bands and villages.
Cyril Radcliffe drew the Punjab and Bengal lines in five weeks; they were published two days after independence.
Communities that found themselves on the wrong side fled or were attacked as they moved.
Violence by local militias did not merely follow partition, it made it, cleansing territory and fixing new identities.
Massacres drove whole districts of Punjab to flee in foot columns and refugee trains.
One of the largest migrations in history followed as minorities crossed the new borders.
A Muslim-majority princely state with a Hindu ruler became the first battlefield between the new dominions.
Losing India removed the Indian Army, the hinge of British power east of Suez, and set the precedent.
